KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Strainer — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the strainer beside its cousin: same idea as the colander, finer net — demonstrated with a snowfall of icing sugar that no child forgets.

What is this?

A strainer is the fine mesh net on a handle — holes so small they catch flour lumps and tea leaves, letting only liquid slip through.

What does it mean?

Strainer and colander make a compare-and-contrast pair: same job, different hole size, different catches. Understanding "the mesh chooses what passes" is early engineering.

What does the child need to know?

You need both tools and a test: which catches flour? Which catches pasta? Then the showstopper — icing sugar shaken through the strainer: snowfall.

Why this matters

The pair teaches by difference: one tool, two hole sizes, two results. Children who can explain WHY the mesh works have engineering thinking — and icing-sugar snowfalls are unbeatable theater.

What it teaches

Comparative thinking (hole sizes), sift-and-strain vocabulary, fine observation, and the flour-lump problem-solving the sieve solves.

Words to learn

strainermeshfinesiftsnowfallcatch

Say this to your child

“"Strainer! The fine net with the handle — the colander’s careful cousin. Flour test: the colander lets it fall, the strainer CATCHES it. And the magic: tap tap tap — sugar SNOW on the cake! Same idea, finer holes."”

Step by step

  1. The cousins together: "strainer and colander — same idea! But look at the holes."
  2. The test: flour into each — "the colander lets it fall! The strainer catches it. The mesh is finer."
  3. The job: "the strainer catches lumps and seeds — only the smooth stuff passes."
  4. The showstopper: icing sugar in the strainer, tapped over a cake — "SNOW! The mesh makes sugar snow."
  5. The verdict: "same idea, finer net. Choose your tool by what you catch."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "strainer" sits over a fine-mesh sieve with a green handle — the mesh woven tight enough to catch a snowfall.

Ask your child

"What does the mesh catch?" (lumps, seeds, flour) "How is it different from the colander?" (finer holes!) "What does it make on the cake?" (sugar snow!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might sift everything (flour, sand, glitter requests), explain the mesh to guests, or request "snow cake" — the pair, understood.

Out in the real world

Strainers sift in tea cultures worldwide — and pools, and paint shops. "A mesh that chooses what passes" appears everywhere once named.

Try it together

Mesh Lab: strainer vs colander vs plate — flour, rice, water through each. Chart what passes, what stays. The lab report is a drawing; the scientist is five.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the strainer catch?" (the fine bits) "Who is its cousin?" (the colander) "What makes snow?" (icing sugar through the mesh!)

This lesson pairs with the Strainer flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.
